title: Hadwiger’s conjecture
formal: Is the following proposition true? For every integer \(n\ge1\), every simple undirected graph \(G\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and every integer \(t\ge1\), if \(\chi(G)\ge t\), then \(G\) contains \(K_t\) as an ordinary graph minor. Equivalently, \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every such graph, where \(h\) is the Hadwiger number defined below.
definitions: The edge set of \(G\) is any set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices in \([n]\); there are no loops or parallel edges. For an integer \(r\ge1\), a proper \(r\)-coloring is a map \(c:[n]\to\{1,\ldots,r\}\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least such \(r\); it exists and lies between \(1\) and \(n\). The graph \(K_t\) has \(t\) vertices and every possible edge. A \(K_t\) minor in \(G\) means that there are \(t\) pairwise disjoint nonempty vertex sets \(B_1,\ldots,B_t\) with both of the following properties: for every \(i\), any two vertices of \(B_i\) are joined by a finite path of edges of \(G\) whose vertices all lie in \(B_i\); and for every \(i<j\), some edge of \(G\) has one endpoint in \(B_i\) and one in \(B_j\). A singleton is connected. The branch sets may have any sizes, need not cover all vertices, and have no restrictions on extra internal edges or on parity. This is equivalent to obtaining \(K_t\) by vertex deletions, edge deletions and edge contractions, discarding loops and merging parallel edges after contraction. It is neither an induced-minor nor an odd-minor requirement. The Hadwiger number \(h(G)\) is the largest \(t\) admitting these branch sets, so \(1\le h(G)\le n\). For \(t\ge2\), the proposition equivalently says that absence of a \(K_t\) minor implies a proper \((t-1)\)-coloring; the \(t=1\) assertion holds automatically for a nonempty graph. Relabeling vertices has no effect. The quantifiers impose no connectedness, degree, order or other restriction on \(G\), and no running-time bound on finding a coloring or a minor.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition for all finite nonempty simple undirected graphs and all integers \(t\ge1\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: existence of a finite graph \(G\) and integer \(t\ge1\) with \(\chi(G)\ge t\) and no \(t\) branch sets satisfying the definition. A counterexample must certify both the chromatic lower bound and absence of the ordinary clique minor. A proof of \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every graph is an equivalent positive answer. No efficient algorithm is required. A constant-factor or asymptotic coloring bound, a finite list of established values of \(t\), a restricted graph class, or a counterexample only to the odd-minor variant does not cover the target.
why: Hadwiger’s conjecture proposes an exact relation between two basic graph parameters: the number of colors needed and the size of a complete graph obtainable by contraction. It extends the Four-Color Theorem and would turn exclusion of a complete minor into the sharp universal coloring bound. Its significance comes from this structural connection across all finite graphs, rather than from an algorithmic requirement in the question.

importance.reason: One of the central graph-theoretic conjectures, with an exact extremal target and consequences across coloring and minor structure.

progress.text: Hadwiger’s original conjecture is restated in the introduction of the cited modern paper; the 1943 original was not inspected in this review.
Kostochka and Thomason establish the \(O(t\sqrt{\log t})\) degeneracy bound, summarized in Theorem 1.3 of Delcourt and Postle. Its tightness concerns degeneracy, not the conjectured chromatic bound.

Robertson, Seymour and Thomas establish the structural result that, with the Four-Color Theorem, proves five-colorability of \(K_6\)-minor-free graphs. The institutional abstract and publication metadata were checked.
Delcourt and Postle obtain \(O(t\log\log t)\) colors. The first preprint was submitted on 3 August 2021, the inspected version 5 on 5 March 2024, and the journal article appeared in 2025.

Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner and Wigderson’s Theorem 1.3 disproves the odd Hadwiger conjecture; their ordinary-minor Conjecture 1.1 remains a separate target. The preprint result is also cited in Liu and Luo’s September 2026 introduction.

Liu and Luo’s version 2 claims \(O(t\log\log\log t)\) colors in Theorem 1.1 and explicitly retains the ordinary Hadwiger conjecture as open. The arXiv version history still lists version 2 as latest on 14 September 2026; the proof was not independently verified.

status_note: The ordinary Hadwiger conjecture is explicitly open in Liu–Luo v2 of 9 September 2026, still its latest arXiv version on 14 September. Its triple-logarithmic coloring theorem is a recent preprint claim, not independently verified here. The December 2025 disproof and its September 2026 citation concern the stronger odd-minor version. Checked source formulations and a bounded later-work search do not certify all cited proofs.

context_blocks.text: A complete minor can be much larger than any complete subgraph: contraction groups connected regions into single vertices. Hadwiger asks whether the resulting complete graph can always have as many vertices as the original graph needs colors. For every \(t\ge2\), the graph \(K_{t-1}\) has no \(K_t\) minor and needs exactly \(t-1\) colors, so the conjectured bound for the excluded-minor class is sharp.

The exact cases through \(t=6\) are known. The \(t=5\) case is equivalent, via Wagner’s theorem, to the Four-Color Theorem for planar graphs. Robertson, Seymour and Thomas established the \(t=6\) case: without assuming four-colorability, their structural result makes a minimal counterexample apex, meaning that deleting one vertex leaves a planar graph. The Four-Color Theorem then gives five colors for that graph. Their paper indexes the conjecture by the allowed number of colors, one less than the clique-minor order used on this card.

Kostochka and Thomason obtained an \(O(t\sqrt{\log t})\) bound on degeneracy, where a graph is \(d\)-degenerate if every nonempty subgraph has a vertex of degree at most \(d\). Such a graph is \((d+1)\)-colorable. The order of this degeneracy bound is tight, but that fact is not a chromatic lower bound of the same order and does not disprove Hadwiger. Delcourt and Postle’s Theorem 1.5 gives \(O(t\log\log t)\) colors for arbitrary \(K_t\)-minor-free graphs; its quantification has no bound on the number of vertices.

Liu and Luo’s version 2, submitted on 9 September 2026, states in Theorem 1.1 that an absolute constant \(C\) satisfies \(\chi(G)\le Ct\log\log\log t\) for every integer \(t\ge16\) and every \(K_t\)-minor-free graph. Their logarithms are natural. This is recorded as a recent preprint claim whose proof has not been independently verified here. It does not establish either the weakening \(\chi(G)=O(t)\) or the exact bound \(t-1\); the introduction still identifies clique-minor orders starting at seven as open.

For the odd-minor variant, the disjoint branch trees must each have a proper two-coloring, with an edge joining vertices of the same color between every pair of trees. Forgetting these extra requirements yields an ordinary minor, so absence of an ordinary minor implies absence of an odd minor; the reverse implication need not hold. Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner and Wigderson’s December 2025 preprint states that for each fixed \(\delta>0\) and every sufficiently large \(t\), some graph has no odd \(K_t\) minor and has \(\chi(G)\ge(3/2-\delta)t\). This refutes the stronger odd-minor conjecture. Odd-minor absence by itself does not certify the ordinary-minor absence required for a negative answer here.

sentences: Hadwiger’s conjecture says that a finite graph needing at least t colors always contains a complete graph on t vertices as a minor.
Such a minor consists of disjoint nonempty connected vertex sets with an edge between every pair of sets.
There are no parity requirements, restrictions on the sizes of these sets, or algorithmic running-time requirements.
The conjecture would extend the Four-Color Theorem to an exact relation between coloring and clique minors in all finite graphs.
A solution must prove the full assertion or certify a finite counterexample in Lean; the recent coloring improvement and the disproof for odd minors do not settle this target.
